title: Area by counting squares
examples: How do I know if I need to use whole or half squares?
Is estimating always the best way to find the area?
What if the shape is really curvy?

explain.say: Today we are learning about finding area by counting squares. We can use whole squares and half squares to help us. Look at this first shape on the screen. It is covered by whole squares only. You can simply count each square to find the total area. This shape has six whole squares covering it. So the area is six square units.

Sometimes the shape does not fit whole squares perfectly. We must use half squares for those tricky spots. Imagine a shape that needs one extra square cut in half. You can count that as one half square. This shape uses three whole squares and two half squares. The total area is three and a half square units.

Estimating helps us guess the area before counting every single square. Look at this next shape. You do not need to count every piece. You can estimate by seeing how many squares fit inside. You might guess it is close to eight square units. Estimation gives us a very good starting idea.

To estimate, we look at the longest side and the shortest side. We can multiply these rough numbers to get an estimate. If the sides are about four and three units, we estimate the area is twelve square units. This gives us a quick answer.

faq.q: When should I use half squares instead of whole squares?
faq.a: You should use half squares when the edge of the shape cuts through a square in the middle. This means the square is only partially covered by the shape. You might also ask, 'Do I always need to use half squares?' or 'When is a half square useful?'
asks: Do I always need to use half squares?
When is a half square useful?

faq.q: Is estimating always the best way to find the area?
faq.a: No, estimating is a good first guess, but counting squares is more exact. Use estimation when you are in a hurry or the shape is very messy. You might also ask, 'Is guessing okay for area?' or 'Should I always count?'

faq.q: What if the shape is really curvy like a circle?
faq.a: For very curvy shapes, counting squares becomes very hard. You might need to use more advanced formulas later on. For now, try to count as many whole squares as possible. You might also ask, 'How do I find the area of a circle?' or 'What about curved shapes?'
asks: How do I find the area of a circle?

faq.q: Can I estimate the area by just looking at the corners?
faq.a: No, you must look at the overall length and the overall width. Think about the shape as a rectangle for a first guess. You might also ask, 'Do I only look at the corners?' or 'Is length and width enough?'
asks: Do I only look at the corners?

faq.q: What is the difference between area and perimeter?
faq.a: Perimeter is the distance around the outside edge of the shape. Area is the space covering the inside of the shape. You might also ask, 'Is area the same as the outside line?' or 'What is the difference between area and perimeter?'
asks: Is area the same as the outside line?
What is the difference between area and perimeter?

facts: Area measures the amount of space inside a two-dimensional shape.
When counting squares, the unit of area is always 'square units'.
A half square is exactly one half of a whole square.
Estimation gives you a close guess, but counting gives the exact answer.

quiz.say: A shape is covered by 5 whole squares and 3 half squares. What is the total area?
quiz.why: You add the whole squares and then count the halves together. Three halves make one and a half, so you add one and a half to five.

wrong.0: This is tempting because you multiply the whole squares by two.
wrong.2: This is tempting because you count all the numbers (5 plus 3) without remembering the halves are parts of a square.
wrong.3: This is tempting because you treat the half squares as if they were whole squares.

quiz.say: If a rectangular area is about 7 units long and 4 units wide, what is a good estimate for its area?
quiz.why: For a quick estimate, you multiply the rough length by the rough width. Seven times four equals twenty-eight.

wrong.1: This is tempting because you only add the length and the width together.
wrong.2: This is tempting because you forget to write the word 'square' after the number.
wrong.3: This is tempting because you only multiply the length by three instead of four.

quiz.say: A shape has a length of 6 units and a width of 3 units. If you estimate the area, what is the best guess?
quiz.why: To estimate the area, you multiply the length by the width. Six multiplied by three equals eighteen.

wrong.0: This is tempting because you only add the length and the width together.
wrong.1: This is tempting because you forget to write the word 'square' after the number.
wrong.2: This is tempting because you mix up the concept of estimation with using only half squares.
